meta.description: Not Disraeli. Quote Investigator traces the quip to Lord Melbourne, aimed at Thomas Babington Macaulay, in print by 1851 — the Disraeli version dates to 1944.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I Wish I Was As Sure of Any One Thing As He is of Everything'?
meta.ogDescription: Lord Melbourne said it about the historian Macaulay. The Disraeli-to-Gladstone version only appears in a 1944 joke book. The full paper trail, 1839 to 1964.

answer.label: Not Disraeli — actually Lord Melbourne
answer.authorDates: 1779–1848 · British Prime Minister; the barb was aimed at Thomas Babington Macaulay
answer.sourceLine: Disraeli almost certainly never said it. Quote Investigator ↗ traces the quip to Lord Melbourne, who aimed it at the historian Thomas Babington Macaulay, famous for being certain about everything — a partial version was in print by 1839 and the first strong match by 1851. The Disraeli-to-Gladstone telling appears only in 1944, in Bennett Cerf’s joke book Try and Stop Me. Melbourne’s exact words are not recoverable: the line survives in half a dozen competing Victorian wordings, and the popular modern form simply swaps a generic “he” for “Tom Macaulay.”

source.excerpt: It was Lord Melbourne, not Sydney Smith, who said, ‘I wish I was as cock-sure of anything as Tom Macaulay is of everything’; but we see now that he had had his own period of cock-sureness like most other people.
trail: 1839 — Quote Investigator ↗ finds an incomplete version in The Quarterly Review, credited to Melbourne but with no target named: “He’s clever enough; but I don’t like those fellows that are always cock-sure of everything.”

1851 — the first strong match, in Graham’s Magazine, introduces it as Melbourne’s hit at Macaulay’s “universal dogmatism”: “I wish that I knew any thing as well as Tom Macaulay knows every thing.” See the chronology ↗
1860 — ten days after Macaulay’s death on 28 December 1859, the 7 January Illustrated London News prints the wording closest to today’s, as transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗.
1889 — Earl Cowper puts it on the record in his preface to Lord Melbourne’s Papers, correcting the rival credit to Sydney Smith. Read the scan ↗
source.excerptNote: Earl Cowper’s preface to Lord Melbourne’s Papers (1889), confirmed in the Internet Archive scan ↗; Quote Investigator gives the page as xii. The wording closest to the popular modern form is the 7 January 1860 Illustrated London News, transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗ as: “I wish that I was as sure of any one thing as—Tom Macaulay is sure of everything”.

source.rightsNote: Every documented printing of this remark is Victorian and long out of copyright in the United States: the 1851 Graham’s Magazine notice, the 7 January 1860 Illustrated London News item, and Earl Cowper’s 1889 preface to Lord Melbourne’s Papers ↗, whose Internet Archive scan records no visible copyright notice. The popular modern wording is simply the 1860 sentence with “Tom Macaulay” replaced by “he,” so no copyrightable modern authorship attaches to it.

author.name: William Lamb, 2nd Viscount Melbourne
author.kicker: The man who actually said it
author.heading: Lord Melbourne, the reluctant wit
author.metaLine: 1779–1848 · British Prime Minister and Queen Victoria’s first political mentor
author.bio: William Lamb, 2nd Viscount Melbourne was a Whig statesman who served as Prime Minister briefly in 1834 and again from 1835 to 1841, and who spent hours a day tutoring the young Queen Victoria in statecraft. He was a famous sceptic in an age of enthusiasts — languid, worldly, allergic to certainty — which is exactly why the jibe fits him. His one lasting contribution to the dictionary of quotations is a complaint about somebody else’s confidence, and even that survives only secondhand, in other people’s memoirs and prefaces.

copyAttribution: "I wish I was as cock-sure of anything as Tom Macaulay is of everything." — attributed to Lord Melbourne (1779–1848), quoted in Earl Cowper's preface to Lord Melbourne's Papers (1889). Commonly misattributed to Benjamin Disraeli; that version first appears in Bennett Cerf's Try and Stop Me (1944). Verified via Quotle.info

misattribution.heading: A joke with a revolving door of authors
misattribution.intro: Almost no quotation has been reassigned as often as this one. Quote Investigator collects at least five different claimants across 125 years of printing, and Benjamin Disraeli is the latest arrival, not the original.

items.why: Bennett Cerf’s Try and Stop Me (1944) stages the line as a debating-chamber comeback: Gladstone thunders that Disraeli cannot be sure of his facts, and Disraeli replies that he wishes he could be as sure of anything as his opponent is of everything. Quote Investigator ↗ records the anecdote but does not credit the attribution — the remark had been in print under Melbourne’s name since 1851, and Disraeli had been dead since 1881. Wikiquote’s Disraeli page ↗ carries no version of it.

A System of Rhetoric (1884) gave a version to the clergyman-wit Sydney Smith. Five years later Earl Cowper corrected the record in his preface to Lord Melbourne’s Papers ↗, writing that it was Melbourne, not Smith, who said it.
Samuel Arthur Bent’s Short Sayings of Great Men (1882) assigned the line to the politician William Windham, per Quote Investigator ↗. Ralph Keyes flagged the same claim in The Quote Verifier.

In The Fine Art of Political Wit (1964), Adlai Stevenson is recorded believing that Macaulay said it — about Brougham — which inverts the joke entirely, since Macaulay was the man being mocked. See the citation ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: On current evidence Quote Investigator ↗ gives priority to Lord Melbourne, with Macaulay as the target — while noting honestly that several wordings circulate and it is not certain which one Melbourne actually used.

context.heading: Why Macaulay was the obvious target
lead: Thomas Babington Macaulay was the most confident man in Victorian public life. His History of England sold like a novel and his essays settled questions other people were still arguing about, in prose that never once sounded unsure. Contemporaries found this exhilarating and slightly maddening — the 1851 Graham’s Magazine notice that carries the first strong version of this quip introduces it as a comment on Macaulay’s “universal dogmatism.”

Melbourne was the perfect man to puncture it. A sceptic who governed without much conviction that governing changed anything, he had exactly the temperament to find total certainty comic. The joke then did what good jokes do: it detached from its author. Within a generation it was being handed to Sydney Smith, to William Windham, and eventually — once the Disraeli-versus-Gladstone rivalry became the standard stage for any British political zinger — to Disraeli.
detailsBody: The versions Quote Investigator collects are not small variants of one sentence. In 1851 it is “I wish that I knew any thing as well as Tom Macaulay knows every thing.” In January 1860 it is “I wish that I was as sure of any one thing as—Tom Macaulay is sure of everything.” In 1865 and again in 1889 the word is “cocksure.” QI is explicit that it is not certain which wording Melbourne actually used.

The modern form — “I wish I was as sure of any one thing as he is of everything” — is the 1860 wording with the name filed off. That generic “he” is what made the line portable enough to be reassigned to Disraeli in 1944 and, in one 1964 retelling by Adlai Stevenson, to Macaulay himself speaking about Lord Brougham.
context.pull: The line outlived everyone in it, and kept changing whose mouth it was in.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator concludes Lord Melbourne (William Lamb) originated the quip aimed at Thomas Babington Macaulay; first strong match 1851 in Graham's Magazine; partial 1839 version in The Quarterly Review; 1860 Illustrated London News (7 January) and 1860 Hotten biography wordings; 1882 Windham and 1884 Sydney Smith reassignments; 1944 Bennett Cerf 'Try and Stop Me' gives it to Disraeli against Gladstone; 1964 'The Fine Art of Political Wit' records Adlai Stevenson giving it to Macaulay about Brougham; QI states it is not certain which wording Melbourne used.

The 1889 volume Lord Melbourne's Papers (ed. Lloyd C. Sanders, preface by the Earl Cowper, Longmans, Green, London) contains in Cowper's preface: 'It was Lord Melbourne, not Sydney Smith, who said, "I wish I was as cock-sure of anything as Tom Macaulay is of everything"; but we see now that he had had his own period of cock-sureness like most other people.' The Internet Archive scan is full-text and records no visible copyright notice, stated date 1889.

Wikiquote's page for William Lamb, 2nd Viscount Melbourne lists 'I wish I were as cocksure of anything as Tom Macaulay is of everything' under its Attributed section, cited to Lloyd C. Sanders (ed.), Lord Melbourne's Papers (1889), p. xii.
Wikiquote's Benjamin Disraeli page contains no version of this remark (no 'sure of any one thing' or 'cocksure' quotation appears on it).

William Lamb, 2nd Viscount Melbourne lived 15 March 1779 – 24 November 1848, was a British Whig statesman, served as Prime Minister in 1834 and again 1835–1841, and was political mentor to the young Queen Victoria.

Thomas Babington Macaulay, 1st Baron Macaulay lived 25 October 1800 – 28 December 1859 and was a British historian, poet and Whig politician; his best-known work is The History of England from the Accession of James the Second.
Benjamin Disraeli lived 21 December 1804 – 19 April 1881 and was a British Conservative statesman and writer who twice served as Prime Minister.
Try and Stop Me (1944) is a best-selling anecdote and humour collection by American publisher Bennett Cerf, originally published by Simon & Schuster.
